participants: Chris Klevan (sales lead, ran the meeting)
Andrew Musial — speaker label "Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)" (closer)
summary: Daily sales team meeting: wins, weekly projections by rep, setter KPI review, then a group call-review session in which Chris Klevan coached Andrew Musial line by line through a recording of a closed call with a prospect named Thomas Joseph. The setters were dismissed partway through so the closers could review the recording. Andrew reported five units and $20,000 cash collected for the week, against $28,000 of contract value, and the meeting closed with a discussion of who the company is actually targeting. This file is unusually valuable because it independently corroborates, and in two places corrects, the sales records for three separate calls in this batch.
notable: TARGETING CONTRADICTION. Asked directly who the company is targeting, Chris Klevan said: "We're targeting people essentially who have like their entire life put together, except fitness. Like guys in their 40s, 50s... they have life together, they might have some injuries, they might have some things, and they need help to actually, like, get their health in order. Like, they need to lose maybe 20, 30, 40 pounds." The ICP as stated to prospects on live calls says the opposite: "It's not like we have dudes who come here who are 50 pounds overweight, who are just like, I need to just lose weight." Internally the sweet spot is 20-40 lb overweight men with injuries; externally prospects are told that is not who they take.

The same statement makes injuries part of the target profile — "they might have some injuries, they might have some things" — which makes the complete absence of any clinical screening step in the sales process materially more serious rather than incidental.

A closer who had just booked five deals in a week did not know the target profile and had to ask: "my question is, who are we targeting right now?" He had formed his own hypothesis (doctors and dentists, because of back pain) and was told those are not the main target.

CASH MAXIMISATION COACHING. Chris Klevan on how to handle a prospect asking about monthly payments: "I would open wallet him and figure out exactly what sort of payment plan he would need to make work. Because that's how you collect the most cash out from somebody that you can collect... maybe you find out he could have piffed, and he has $20,000 on a credit card, then you find out, dude, just put it on a credit card, piff it."

PAYMENT PLAN PREMIUM CONFIRMED AND ITS USE CRITICISED. The rep had told the prospect "you could, but it's going to be a little bit more expensive... it's not going to be 1k per month. It's going to be 1,200." Chris's correction was about framing, not about the premium: "You went right into telling him what it would be and using the interest against him to want to pay more. So you use interest as the thing as to why he should do it, which I don't really love that frame." The $1,200/month figure is therefore a standard rate, not an improvisation.

TAMER DEAL REPORTED AS SECURED. Andrew described the previous day's three-month close to the team as effectively a six-month deal: "He got in for three months, but he will do the six months... He was just making sure that if it's going to be what I said, that after those three months, he will only top up with the 2K, that is secured, yeah?" Nobody asked whether the arrangement was documented. The agreement that prospect signed covers three months only.

SETTER ATTRIBUTION RECOVERED. Kyla Louie claimed the Tamer deal as her win — "my win is my deal yesterday with Andrew" — which establishes she set that appointment even though the file title carries no KL suffix. She did not remember the prospect's name: "That was his name?"

WEEKLY NUMBERS ON RECORD. Andrew: "Monday was 6K, Wednesday was 6K with two pay, then was one piff, 6K split in two, and the 4K split in two." Five units, $28,000 contract value, $20,000 cash. The $4,000 split-in-two is the Tamer deal; the PIF at $6,000 is the prospect who asked about merchandise, which identifies him as Patrick Soldow.

WHATSAPP PRACTICE IS SANCTIONED. Andrew described giving prospects his private WhatsApp number at the end of most calls and Chris approved it — "Yeah, I don't see an issue with that" — while suggesting a better framing that keeps Trevor as the coach.

ETHNIC PROFILING OF A CLIENT. Andrew explained his read on the prospect: "he's also half Indian, I think. So work for them is always a priority." Chris followed with a remark about the prospect's name.

COACHING AGAINST PERSONAL STORIES. Chris told Andrew repeatedly not to share his own boxing and hiking stories early in discovery — "never talk about yourself. Just don't do it" — calling the close a "false positive". Andrew uses that story routinely; it appears in at least three prospect calls in this batch.

SETTER KPI STATED: "I need to see 120 dials or four sets" per day. Kyla admitted missing it — "I just haven't done it. It's a bad excuse. I haven't put in the volume" — and was held to it without penalty.

Kim Forbes-Sobers described nurturing a prospect he had disqualified the previous week on affordability by sending free resources, and the prospect came back warm. Financial disqualification is treated as reversible.
Call recordings are stored in a Slack channel named call-recording-sales, which is where the team reviews closes.

The reviewed prospect, Thomas Joseph, is a 39-year-old psychiatrist, 5'8" and 187 lb, targeting mid-160s and 10-12% body fat, with a 20-month-old and another child due in December. He closed on a two-payment $6,000 deal. He disclosed pulling his back deadlifting around 220-245 lb roughly a year to eighteen months earlier and never having it diagnosed, but stated he is pain-free and can do all lifts. Notably, this is the one call in the corpus so far where the rep did ask injury and chronic-condition screening questions directly. That call's own recording is not in this batch.

Chris explicitly frames prospects with a baby on the way as higher-probability closes: "It doesn't matter what the offer is. If there's a baby on the way, it's, like, such a higher chance they're going to close." And psychiatrists: "psychiatrists usually also are pretty good I've found to close them, because they do, like, the deep inner work... it's very easy to speak to them about beliefs."
